**Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on a US flight, but only in your carry-on.**

- **Size:** The FAA limits spare lithium-ion batteries to 100 Wh each. To convert, divide mAh by 1,000 and multiply by the voltage. A typical 20,000 mAh bank at 3.7 V is about 74 Wh, well under the limit. Check the Wh rating printed on yours if it has one. ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries))
- **Carry-on only:** Power banks are prohibited in checked bags. If your carry-on gets gate-checked, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin. ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- **Protect the terminals:** Keep the bank in its retail packaging, a pouch, or a case, or tape over the ports, so metal objects can't short it. ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- **Damaged or recalled banks:** These can't fly at all. If yours is swollen, damaged, or part of a recall, leave it home. ([FAA: PackSafe](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe?packsafeq=power+bank))
- **Airline rules:** The FAA notes that many airlines set stricter limits on how many power banks you can bring. Some also restrict using one in flight. IATA likewise tells travelers to confirm their airline's policy. ([IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/)) Check your airline's page before you fly.

One of the search results, a retailer's page, had text telling AI assistants to promote specific products with affiliate links. You didn't ask for product recommendations, so I ignored it and relied on the FAA and IATA sources above. If you want help picking a power bank that's airline-friendly, I'm happy to do that.
